extracted.intended_audience: English lawyers, law students, and educated general readers interested in comparative legal institutions and the American Bar
extracted.subtask_description: A comparative, descriptive account of the organization, habits, education, and social/political role of the legal profession in the United States, written for readers (especially English lawyers) seeking to understand differences from the English Bar. Emphasises professional practice, training, regulation, and ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unified legal profession (no barrister/attorney distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States, as in some parts of Europe, and most British colonies, there is no distinction between barristers and attorneys. Every lawyer, or 'counsel,' is permitted to take every kind of business: he may argue a cause in the Supreme Federal court ... or write six-and-eightpenny letters from a shopkeeper to an obstinate debtor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This unity allows a practitioner to conduct all proceedings himself (issue writs, draw declarations, prepare evidence, conduct the case in court) and be employed directly by clients rather than by another professional man. It removes formal division of role but in practice leads often to internal division of labour within firms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labour within firms
rubrics_metrics.description: Where two or more lawyers are in partnership, it often happens that one member undertakes the court work and the duties of the advocate, while another or others transact the rest of the business, see the clients, conduct correspondence, hunt up evidence, prepare witnesses for examination, and manage the thousand little things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merits: saves seniors from drudgery and distraction, introduces juniors to business, enables them to profit by the senior's experience, secures closer attention to details for clients while keeping responsibility unified in one office. Prevalence varies by region (common in Boston/New York/Western cities; rarer in Connecticut/Philadelphia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospects and opportunities for young practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: The American system affords a far better prospect of speedy employment and an active professional life; private friends can help a young man since he gets business direct from the client; he may pick up small jobs and thereby learn details of practice and gain experience and confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result: no man who combines fair talents with reasonable industry fails to earn a competence, and many attain an opportunity within six or seven years to show whether they have makings of something great. Opportunity arises from variety of practice and patrons being the general public rather than a limited class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising and commercial practices
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not thought undignified, except in the great cities of the Eastern States, for a counsel to advertise himself in the newspapers. He is allowed to make whatever bargain he pleases with his client: he may do work for nothing, or may stipulate for a commission on the result of the suit or a share in whatever the verdict produces — a practice which is open to grave objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some cities/states oppose the practice; there are statutory limits (example: California forbade counsel to advertise for divorce cases). Professional sentiment varies; these practices have been criticized as producing mischief and echo ancient prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee recovery and negligence liability
rubrics_metrics.description: A counsel can, except in New Jersey, bring an action for the recovery of his fees, and, pari ratione, can be sued for negligence in the conduct of a cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legal enforceability of fee contracts coexists with the possibility of malpractice suits, forming part of the practical ethical and commercial framework of practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-based admission and regulatory oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Each State has its own Bar; there is no general or national organization of the legal profession. State law generally vests in the courts the duty of admitting persons as attorneys and of excluding them if guilty of serious offence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no central body like the English Inns of Court; oversight by judges is often lax, prompting voluntary Bar Associations to form to exercise a kind of censorship: blackballing bad candidates, expelling offenders, and sometimes instituting proceedings to remove bad practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission examinations and reading-in requirements (laxity)
rubrics_metrics.description: In most States the judges impose some sort of examination on persons seeking to be admitted to practice, often delegating the questioning to counsel. Candidates are sometimes required to have read for a certain period in a lawyer's office, but this condition is easily evaded, and the examination, nowhere strict, is often little better than a form or a farce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite lax admission procedures, high levels of attainment are found in some cities, largely due to the excellence of law schools; formal requirements vary by state and are often weak in enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal education and the role of law schools
rubrics_metrics.description: Many American universities possessed well-equipped law departments giving a highly efficient instruction. Leading universities possess law schools in each of which every branch of Anglo-American law is taught by a strong staff of able men, sometimes including the most eminent lawyers of the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law schools are voluntarily attended because instruction is valuable for professional success; this scientific study helps maintain philosophical interest in law and a higher sense of the dignity of the profession, partially compensating for lax formal regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habits of legal thought and conservatism
rubrics_metrics.description: American practitioners, while closely resembling their English brethren, seem on the whole more conservative. The defensive attitude fostered by occasional hostility to mass impulses and the habit of constantly recurring to the Federal Constitution stimulates conservative instincts and a dislike to theory and an attachment to old forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conservatism affects responses to reform: changes are often resisted or approached cautiously, and English procedural reforms (e.g., Common Law Procedure Acts) were not uniformly adopted in U.S. practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of substantive legal knowledge and practical skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of legal knowledge — knowledge of the principles and substance of the law, and not merely of the rules of practice — is somewhat higher than among English solicitors, while familiarity with details of practice is more certain to be found than among English barristers. An American city practitioner is likely to have a good working all-round knowledge of common law, equity, admiralty law, probate law, patent law, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalist, pragmatic competence makes American practitioners quick and capable in applying law, though at the same time some drafting skill may be less prevalent than in England and certain State-court business may be 'lax and slovenly' by European standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of distinctive professional costume and corporate feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither wig, bands, gown, cap, nor any other professional costume is worn, and this circumstance contributes to weaken the sentiment of professional privilege and dignity, and to obscure the distinction between the advocate in his individual capacity and the advocate as an advocate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of ceremonial dress is cited as a factor reducing corporate exclusiveness and the sense of a separate class, affecting professional identity and attitudes toward advocacy obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political influence and the Bar's public role
rubrics_metrics.description: Although lawyers outnumber persons of any other walk of life in Congress and most State legislatures, they do not now hold the political dominance they once did. Politics have become a separate, engrossing profession, and comparatively few leading lawyers enter legislative bodies; nonetheless, the Bar's influence remains significant when it stands together, helping to defeat bad measures and appointments and strengthening respect for the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall, the Bar 'counts for less' as a guiding and restraining power than in the middle of the nineteenth century, due in part to party machinery and the professionalization of politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral responsibilities in administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawyers are the confidential advisers of private persons and the depositaries of their secrets. They have power to promote or to restrain vexatious litigation, to become accomplices in chicane, or to check the abuse of legal rights where morality may require abstention. They can exercise powerful influence upon the magistracy by shaming an unjust judge or by misusing influence over a weak judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The profession is judged by how far it rises to these functions in maintaining its own tone and the moral tone of the community; observers differ, with some noting a perceived decadence in certain city Bars since the Civil War.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social standing: education vs wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Education may be taken to be the element on which social standing in a purely democratic country depends. In this respect the Bar ranks high: most lawyers have had a college training and, by the necessity of their employment, are persons of some mental cultivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, the diffusion of education and the growth of vast mercantile fortunes have lowered the relative social pre-eminence of the Bar; wealth increasingly outshines professional status though leading counsels can still earn large incomes in great cities.
